set.hook: Family-run Lapad kitchen near the Eden hotel that rolls its own pasta and sauces, Italian more than Dalmatian.
set.why: Up on Kardinala Stepinca in Lapad, away from the walls and the cruise crowds, this small family room built its name on pasta made in the house and sauces invented to go with it. Time Out filed it as an Italian table, and the reviews that keep coming back name the paella and a big bowl of mussels. A June 2026 city listing calls it Atlantic Cucina Italiana, which tells you where the kitchen's heart is.
set.verdict: Worth the taxi to Lapad if it is still trading, but that is the open question: one TripAdvisor page now tags it closed while a listing updated in June 2026 still gives daily hours. Phone before you send anyone. When it works, it is a fair-priced plate of house pasta in a quiet street, with no view to pay for.
set.signature: House-made pasta with the sauce of the day.
set.caveat: Trading status unclear in 2026 (TripAdvisor flags it closed); call +385 20 435 726 before going.

set.hook: Bosnian family kitchen inside the walls, MICHELIN Bib Gourmand, grilled meat from its own butcher.
set.why: The name has nothing to do with India: this is the Old Town's Bosnian house, on Nikole Gučetića just off the Stradun. MICHELIN lists it as a Bib Gourmand and says the meat on the grill comes from the family's own butcher, and the plum baklava is made by the owner's mother. There is a second, roomier branch in Hotel Lero, a few kilometres up toward Gruž, for nights the alley is full.
set.verdict: Good-value Balkan cooking with a guide's backing, in a part of town where value is rare. Expect meat, kajmak and bread in quantity, not seafood. Book: the small room fills, and MICHELIN itself advises reservations. A sound last-minute table for crew or guests who are tired of grilled fish.
set.signature: The Taj Mahal special: veal with mushrooms in a crisp pastry shell.
set.caveat: Small and popular, book ahead; winter hours not confirmed, call +385 20 323 221.

set.hook: Old Town wine bar off the Stradun pouring Croatian bottles by the glass and in tasting flights.
set.why: D'vino sits on Palmotićeva, one of the stepped lanes north of the Stradun, and was built around one idea: let a visitor taste the country without buying bottles. The bar's own site claims more than 60 wines by the glass, the largest such list in Dubrovnik, and the flights of Croatian whites and reds come with English notes. Total Croatia News names Sasha Lušić as the owner who runs the room.

set.hook: Mike Grgich's Pelješac homecoming above Trstenik: two wines, Plavac Mali and Pošip, tasted side by side.
set.why: Miljenko Grgich left Croatia, made the Chardonnay that won the 1976 Paris tasting, and came back in 1996 to build a winery on the headland above Trstenik. It still makes just two wines, and the tasting covers both. Falstaff tasted them in April 2026 and gave the 2022 Plavac Mali and the 2024 Pošip 93 points each, and lists the house in its 2026 guide.
set.verdict: A short, focused visit rather than a long estate tour: two glasses, a view over the Trstenik bay and a story every wine-minded guest will know. Pair it with lunch on Pelješac. Outside July and August the family-run schedule can slip, and nobody may be free to guide you; ring first.
set.signature: The Plavac Mali next to the Pošip.
set.caveat: Call ahead outside peak season; Time Out gives April–November only.

set.hook: The Miloš family's organic Plavac Mali house at Ponikve, maker of Stagnum, tasted in a rock-cut room.
set.why: Above Ston at Ponikve, the Miloš family farms Plavac Mali organically and ages its top red, Stagnum, in large old Slavonian oak. Hugh Johnson called it the first Croatian cult wine. Falstaff's Peter Moser tasted the 2016 in April 2026, scored it 94 and called it a traditional icon of the peninsula. The tasting room is built into the rock of the hillside.
set.verdict: The serious red stop on Pelješac, for guests who want to taste aged Plavac Mali rather than the fresh style. Tastings are quiet and unhurried. Fit it on the way back from Ston oysters; book in advance, since this is a family house, not a visitor centre.

set.hook: Gruž harbour's open market and fish hall, where boats from the Elafiti land the morning catch.
set.why: On the Gruž waterfront, opposite the ferry and cruise berths, the city's working market sells produce from the Konavle and Rijeka Dubrovačka growers outdoors and fish under cover. Time Out says the fish comes in from the Elafiti islands and to arrive by seven for the best of it. Absolute Croatia says Friday and Saturday are the busiest days, and that prices soften toward closing.
set.verdict: The provisioning stop for any boat lying in Gruž: real fish, real vegetables, cash in hand. Go early, because the fish hall thins out fast. Do not expect a food hall; it is a market for buying, not for eating.

set.hook: A tiny Old Town sandwich counter: warm house bread, Drniš pršut and Konavle cheese, in Gault&Millau 2026.
set.why: On Antuninska, a stepped lane off the Stradun, Škola does one thing: a sandwich on bread baked in the house, filled with pršut from Drniš in the Dalmatian hinterland and cheese from Konavle south of the city. It made both the Gault&Millau Croatia 2026 and Falstaff 2026 guides, the latter at 82 points, which is rare for a place with three tables. There is a special menu with vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free choices.
set.verdict: The best cheap lunch inside the walls and the quickest: order, eat standing or take it to the harbour. It is not a restaurant and does not pretend to be. Good for crew between jobs and for guests who want one honest local bite between the walls walk and the boat.

set.hook: Old Town seafood counter off the Stradun turning the day's catch into octopus burgers and anchovy sandwiches.

locals.title: Where Dubrovnik eats off-stage
locals.story: When the cruise crowds fill the Stradun, the city eats a few streets away or in the suburbs. Taj Mahal, on Nikole Gučetića inside the walls, is a Bosnian family house with a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand and meat from its own butcher. Pizzeria Tabasco, on Hvarska by the Ploče gate, fires its pizzas in a wood oven and keeps the same hours most of the year. Up in Lapad, Atlantic Kitchen built its reputation on pasta rolled in the house, though one listing now flags it closed, so its status is open. None of the three is about the sea view; they are about price and appetite.
locals.where: Taj Mahal, Old Town; Pizzeria Tabasco, Ploče; Atlantic Kitchen, Lapad

glass.title: Plavac Mali and Pošip
glass.story: South Dalmatia's wine comes mostly from the Pelješac peninsula, an hour north of Dubrovnik, and its red grape is Plavac Mali. Grgić Vina at Trstenik, founded in 1996 by Mike Grgich after his Paris win of 1976, makes just two wines; Falstaff scored both 93 in April 2026. Vinarija Miloš at Ponikve, near Ston, ages its Stagnum in old Slavonian oak, and Falstaff gave the 2016 a 94 the same month. In the Old Town, D'vino on Palmotićeva pours more than 60 Croatian wines by the glass, though it keeps tourist-season months.
glass.where: D'vino, Dubrovnik Old Town; Grgić Vina, Trstenik; Vinarija Miloš, Ponikve

street.title: The market and the bun
street.story: Dubrovnik's cheap food starts at the Gruž market on the harbour, where Time Out says fish from the Elafiti islands is best before seven and Friday and Saturday are the busiest days. Inside the walls, Buffet Škola on Antuninska fills house-baked bread with Drniš pršut and Konavle cheese, and made both Gault&Millau and Falstaff in 2026. Barba, on Boškovićeva, turns octopus, anchovies and shrimp into burgers and sandwiches eaten standing in the lane. The fish hall is cash only, and buying there means cooking on board or handing the bag to a galley. All three are quick and quick, and none takes bookings.
street.where: Gruž Market, Gruž; Buffet Škola, Old Town; Barba, Old Town
